stories.title: Africa: El Niño Threatens More Than Two-Thirds of Children in Eastern and Southern Africa
stories.summary: Africa: El NiÃ±o Threatens More Than Two-Thirds of Children in Eastern and Southern Africa Naftalin/UNICEF 13-year-old Mathiei Makuol collects dirty water from the floodwater in the village of Panyagor in Twic East, Jonglei State in South Sudan. 1 September 2026 United Nations Children's Fund (New York) Nairobi — UNICEF calls for urgent action to protect children from a predictable crisis More than 162 million children, over two-thirds of all children in Eastern and Southern Africa, live in areas exposed to the impact of the strengthening 2026/2027 El Niño, UNICEF warned today. Intensifying drought, extreme heat and flooding threaten children's nutrition, health, access to safe water and sanitation, education and safety. Forecasts provide a narrow but critical window to act before the most severe consequences are felt. "The threat from El Niño is growing, and the risks for children are already clear," said Etleva Kadilli, UNICEF Regional Director for Eastern and Southern Africa. "Across the region, children are facing food and water insecurity, overstretched health services and disrupted learning. Further, major climate shocks will likely push children and the systems they rely on to breaking point." UNICEF assessments point to urgent and overlapping risks for children in Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe. For example, in Somalia, flooding could directly affect up to 2.5 million people under the most severe scenario mapping, driving displacement and impacting children's access to food, healthcare, safe water and education; in Ethiopia, tens of thousands of children are likely to be affected, particularly in areas already facing severe food insecurity and vulnerability; and in South Sudan, drought, extreme heat and localized flooding threaten to deepen food insecurity and malnutrition, increase disease outbreaks and compound famine risks and large-scale displacement.

stories.summary: Malawi: Chilima Plane Crash Inquiry Lays Bare Malawi's Aviation Safety Crisis Saulos Klaus Chilima/Page Facebook Saulos Klaus Chilima 2 September 2026 Nyasa Times (Leeds) By Wongani Chiuta The parliamentary inquiry into the June 10, 2024 plane crash that killed Vice-President Saulos Chilima and eight others has heard troubling testimony suggesting Malawi's aviation infrastructure suffers from long-standing structural deficiencies -- raising uncomfortable questions about institutional readiness that extend well beyond the immediate circumstances of the crash itself. Fredrick Chisepeya, director of Aerodromes and Air Navigation Standards at the Civil Aviation Authority of Malawi (CAAM), told Parliament's Ad-hoc Committee investigating the disaster that the country risks failing next year's International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) audit unless significant investment is urgently directed towards safety and security infrastructure. His testimony painted a picture of a system operating with minimal redundancy: Malawi possesses just one secondary flight surveillance radar, situated at Kamuzu International Airport in Lilongwe, whose effective coverage diminishes substantially for aircraft flying at lower altitudes. It was this gap, Chisepeya confirmed, that meant the Malawi Defence Force aircraft was outside radar coverage entirely when it crashed in Viphya Plantation. stories.summary: Namibia: Drought Displaced Angolans Face Human Rights Abuses 2 September 2026 Amnesty International (London) Angolan women and children displaced by drought into Namibia face serious human rights abuses arising from a lack of safe and legal migration pathways for people forced across borders by natural disasters, Amnesty International said in a new report. The report, " The Drier it Gets, the Longer You Have to Walk: The Human Rights Impacts of Drought-Induced Displacement on Angolan Women and Children in Namibia , documents the devastating consequences of recurrent drought in southern Angola and the human rights impacts experienced by those displaced into Namibia, including persistent fear of arrest, detention and deportation, which in turn influences their daily decisions about whether to seek healthcare and other services. "Namibian authorities must establish a rights-based approach to migration, ensuring that people displaced by drought and other natural disasters can access basic rights, including registration and documentation." Said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International's Regional Director for East and Southern Africa. "The protection of already marginalized Angolans who are forced to move to Namibia in search of livelihoods is not just a humanitarian concern. This is a human rights crisis that demands international solidarity, including legal protection against refoulement," said Tigere Chagutah. stories.title: Tunisia: Tunisia's Rights Defenders Decry Civil Society Crackdown
stories.summary: Tunisia's Rights Defenders Decry Civil Society Crackdown TnPresidency/X Tunisian President Kais Saied. 2 September 2026 Deutsche Welle (Bonn) By Jennifer Holleis Five years into the authoritarian rule of Tunisian President Kais Saied, Human Rights Watch and other activists warn that Tunisia's once vibrant civil society is in danger of being completely stifled. "Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities." Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues. "What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention , the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. "It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights . "The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW. He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

Appearing before the committee chaired by Fredrick Ruhindi, Tumwebaze made an impassioned case for moving away from what he described as a rigid, single-standard Western attire requirement, particularly the business suit, tie and tucked-in shirt. L'ambassadeur russe à Niamey, Viktor Voropayev, avait, le même jour, lui-même mis en avant cette intervention "pour réprimer une mutinerie". "L'Africa Corps a joué un rôle décisif en fournissant un appui terrestre et aérien pour aider les forces loyalistes à reprendre la base aérienne 101, l'un des sites les plus stratégiques de la capitale", affirme à l'AFP Charlie Werb, analyste du cabinet de conseil Aldebaran Threat Consultants (ATC), qui estime que "la mutinerie est le résultat de la dégradation du paysage sécuritaire du Niger ", confronté aux violences jihadistes. The workers' union on Tuesday signed a deal with the government committing to resume work immediately, after talks in which officials agreed to resolve a pay dispute and other grievances that led to the strike. Since Sunday, hundreds of passengers had been stranded at the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), a key regional transport hub, as the nationwide go-slow strike began. The workers were demanding better working conditions and the implementation of a previously agreed deal. "We are simply calling off our strike action and pleading with our members to begin the process of normalising operations, restoring services," Moss Ndiema, the head of the workers' union, told a press conference on Tuesday. "For those who are on duty, we are asking them to begin clearing flights." Transport Minister Davis Chirchir said they had agreed with the union on the way forward to address the grievances that had led to the strike. "It's unfortunate that we had to get here but we are out of it, and it's unfortunate because the loss to the economy, which we don't yet have the numbers, is huge." On Monday, passengers hoping to get on a flight were stuck at JKIA, with some spending the night in and around the check-in areas waiting for news. Kenya Airways said it was experiencing delays of more than six hours, and the flight backlog had forced it to cancel some departures.

stories.summary: Lionel Messi has retired from international football at 39, ending a remarkable 21-year career with Argentina just weeks after leading the team to the 2026 World Cup final. He leaves as the nation’s record appearance holder and top scorer.

stories.title: Comment Emmanuel Ackah est devenu la clé de voûte du système Gbagbo
stories.summary: Comment Emmanuel Ackah est devenu la clé de voûte du système Gbagbo De l’ambassade de Côte d’Ivoire au Ghana en passant par la direction du cabinet du président du PPA-CI, l’ancien footballeur s’est toujours tenu loin des projecteurs. Ce qui ne l’a pas empêché d’acquérir une grande influence. Emmanuel Ackah, directeur de cabinet de Laurent Gbagbo et troisième vice-président du PPA-CI. © DR Par Alain Aka (à Abidjan) Publié aujourd'hui à 19h15 Lecture : 3 minutes. Fichier généré le Lire dans l’app Résumer « Je ne suis pas un homme politique au sens où on l’entend [généralement]. Cela n’a rien de péjoratif [dans ma bouche], mais je ne suis pas un politicien de carrière. » Au sein du Parti des peuples africains – Côte d’Ivoire ( PPA-CI ), le directeur de cabinet de Laurent Gbagbo passe souvent pour énigmatique.

stories.title: Guinea-Bissau votes on stronger presidency as military transition nears end
stories.summary: Guinea-Bissau voted Sunday on a proposed new constitution that would significantly strengthen presidential powers and shrink parliament, in a referendum seen as a test of the military government's bid to reshape the political system before elections scheduled for December.

stories.title: Niger : la nuit où Abdourahamane Tiani a vacillé
stories.summary: Niger : la nuit où Abdourahamane Tiani a vacillé Dans la nuit du 28 au 29 août, des dizaines de militaires ont tenté de prendre d’assaut le palais présidentiel et se sont emparés d’une partie de la base aérienne 101 de Niamey. Un véhicule blindé militaire prend position dans la rue à la suite d’une attaque menée par des mutins contre l’aéroport international et la présidence à Niamey, le 30 août 2026. © REUTERS Par Jeune Afrique Publié aujourd'hui à 18h14, modifié à 18h28 Lecture : 6 minutes. Dans les quartiers proches du Plateau, où se trouvent le palais présidentiel, les principales administrations et la télévision nationale, les habitants sont réveillés par le fracas des armes. stories.title: Chez Castel, la guerre des clans ne faiblit pas
stories.summary: Chez Castel, la guerre des clans ne faiblit pas La guerre de succession au sein du groupe Castel s’emballe. Communiqués contradictoires, révocations contestées et batailles judiciaires : la gouvernance d’un empire présent dans 22 pays africains vacille. Gregory Clerc, l’actuel directeur général du groupe Castel, le 17 octobre 2025. © Christel JEANNE pour JA Par Salimata Koné Publié hier à 17h58, modifié aujourd'hui à 12h04 Lecture : 3 minutes. Fichier généré le Lire dans l’app Résumer Le bras de fer se poursuit au sein de la famille Castel . Par communiqués interposés, les différentes branches de l’actionnariat familial ont de nouveau exposé leurs désaccords sur la place publique, sur fond de bataille autour de la gouvernance du groupe.

stories.title: Ethiopia backs executive presidency plan, raising fears of power grab
stories.summary: Ethiopia’s national dialogue has endorsed constitutional changes that would merge the roles of prime minister and president into a powerful executive presidency, a move critics warn could allow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed to further consolidate his control after his party’s landslide election victory.

stories.title: DRC Ebola outbreak surges past 6,000 cases as death toll nears 3,000
stories.summary: The Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases and killed 2,911 people, making it the country’s largest outbreak on record and one of the fastest-growing Ebola epidemics ever recorded. More than 1,360 people have recovered.

stories.title: En Algérie, face à des incendies d’une ampleur exceptionnelle, la très grande discrétion des autorités
stories.summary: A Jijel et Béjaïa, des incendies d’une violence inédite ont balayé montagnes et littoraux, faisant plus de 200 victimes. Alors que beaucoup s’interrogent sur le niveau d’impréparation de l’Etat, l’exécutif souligne le caractère criminel de certains feux et exige un durcissement de la réponse judiciaire.

stories.title: En déployant ses avions de combat au Niger, l'Algérie veut "prévenir d'éventuelles attaques"
stories.summary: Publicité En déployant ses avions de combat au Niger, l'Algérie veut "prévenir d'éventuelles attaques" Entretien Afrique Pour la première fois, l'Algérie a déployé dimanche des avions de combat au Niger après qu'une mutinerie contre la junte a été déjouée la veille à Niamey. Selon le journaliste spécialisé en défense et sécurité Akram Kharief, Alger veut afficher son soutien aux autorités nigériennes et cherche à lutter contre le terrorisme, sans rompre avec sa doctrine de non-intervention à l'étranger. stories.title: Haiti mourns victims of Kenscoff gang attack as fear grips community
stories.summary: Hundreds of mourners gathered at a church near Haiti’s capital on Sunday to bury victims of a brutal gang attack that killed at least 47 people and left more than 50 others kidnapped. The killings have renewed fears that worsening violence is undoing fragile security gains.

stories.title: Spain PM Pedro Sanchez rules out Moroccan role in Ceuta migrant surge
stories.summary: Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez says there is no evidence that Moroccan authorities were involved in the sudden arrival of more than 70,000 migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta last month.

stories.title: Vincent Bolloré dépose plainte pour « association de malfaiteurs » contre des magistrats, après son renvoi devant le tribunal pour corruption
stories.summary: Dans une ultime tentative d’obtenir le renvoi de son procès pour corruption au Togo, prévu du 7 au 17 décembre au tribunal judiciaire de Paris, le milliardaire a déposé plainte, en mai, contre des magistrats, pour « entrave à l’exercice de la justice ».

stories.title: Algeria president seeks death penalty for arsonists after deadly forest fires
stories.summary: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune said he was not ruling out foul play after 100 wildfires were recorded By Basillioh Rukanga Published 31 August 2026 Updated 1 September 2026 Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has said he wants to reinstate the death penalty for arsonists, following a wave of deadly forest fires. The official death toll stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure is much higher. The president ordered the justice ministry to introduce changes to the criminal law introducing capital punishment for arsonists. Capital punishment remains in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993. More than 100 wildfires have been recorded in recent days in the north-east of the country, most of which have been extinguished.

stories.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pirates manage to board ships operating a long way from the coast and then guide them closer to the shore By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent Published 29 August 2026 Updated 31 August 2026 A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran. Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates. It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade. "Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity." That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north. Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea.

stories.title: How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand
stories.summary: The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub View image in fullscreen The Water Hub’s filter beds remove nearly 99% of toxins before most of the water is released back into the river, with some held back to irrigate gardens. Photograph: Courtesy of Water Hub How a South African town cleaned up its polluted river using stones, wood and sand Scientists say system to treat contaminated wastewater offers a model for ensuring food security in a fast-warming climate A ll it took to turn the murky, heavily polluted waters of South Africa’s Stiebeuel River into a resource clean enough for irrigating a community’s vegetable plots was a collection of stones, heat-treated wood and sand. Without chemicals and using renewable energy, researchers from the University of Cape Town are cleaning 36,000 litres of water, polluted by sewage, chemicals, and traces of drugs and medication, every day to make it usable for growing food in a fast-expanding informal settlement along the course of the river. Scientists behind the project think it could be a model for ensuring food security in the climate crisis. “ What we’re doing is taking that water, treating it every day, and some of that water is now being used for growing vegetables, for feeding hungry children and people living in the informal settlement,” says Kevin Winter, one of the researchers behind the Water Hub project in Langrug , near Stellenbosch in South Africa’s Western Cape region.

stories.title: RDC : quand le cuivre éclipse le cobalt dans la course aux minerais critiques
stories.summary: Hausse du cours du cuivre, restrictions sur les exportations de cobalt : la RDC est à la croisée des chemins. En conséquence, les grands groupes miniers actifs dans le pays pivotent vers le métal rouge, dont la demande mondiale dépasse de loin celle du cobalt.

stories.title: Libye : entre Haftar et Dbeibah, duel pour le Sahel
stories.summary: Du Fezzan au Niger en passant par le Tchad, les deux camps qui se partagent la Libye se disputent réseaux et influence. Du côté du clan Haftar, Saddam, fils et dauphin du maréchal, est à la manœuvre, sur fond de défections et de rivalités intrafamiliales.

stories.title: Notting Hill Carnival kicks off in a burst of colour and Caribbean tradition
stories.summary: London’s Notting Hill Carnival got underway on Sunday with revellers covered in oil and paint as the annual celebration of Caribbean culture and music returned to the British capital. The three-day event is marking its 60th anniversary and is expected to draw millions of visitors.

stories.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
stories.summary: Protesters in London calling for reparations. At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries. stories.title: Sweden ends aid to Liberia in a hammer blow to women’s rights and healthcare
stories.summary: The Swedish embassy shut its doors in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, on 31 August. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy View image in fullscreen The Swedish embassy shut its doors in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, on 31 August. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Sweden ends aid to Liberia in a hammer blow to women’s rights and healthcare Sexual and reproductive services face an uncertain future as the country’s second-largest donor halts support worth hundreds of millions of pounds T he Swedish flag is still flying above the pale blue building overlooking the Atlantic in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, but the doors of the embassy are now closed to visitors. On 31 August, the Swedish embassy in Liberia ends a presence in the country that dates back to 1961. The billions of kronor of aid that Sweden pipes into the west African country will end on the same day, as sweeping cuts to Swedish development funding come into effect.

stories.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
stories.summary: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation. As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration .

stories.title: Pétrole du lac Albert : la RDC peut-elle contester le projet de TotalEnergies en Ouganda ?
stories.summary: Alors que l’entrée en production du projet controversé de la major française est imminente, Kinshasa réclame une exploitation équitable et concertée de l’or noir des zones frontalières.

stories.title: Cameroun : entre le ministre Atanga Nji et l’opposant Kamto, la guerre se poursuit
stories.summary: Le ministre de l’Administration territoriale a apporté son soutien à un dissident du MRC qui conteste la présidence de Maurice Kamto. À l’approche des élections législatives et locales de 2027, l’opposition dénonce une nouvelle tentative de déstabilisation.

stories.title: ‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain
stories.summary: Composite: Soraya Aybar Laafou View image in fullscreen Composite: Soraya Aybar Laafou ‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain More than two dozen teenagers stuck in the Spanish territory of Ceuta shared their reasons for joining the treacherous mass crossing in July For Fatin, one of the teenage girls now living in limbo in a makeshift camp in the Spanish city of Ceuta, the decision to leave her home in Morocco began to form when she had to give up school. She wanted to continue studying, she says, but at home she was expected to take responsibility for the housework instead. As classes and learning gave way to domestic chores, the future she had imagined for herself began to feel increasingly distant. Fatin was one of 29 girls who shared their feelings about their past and future with the Guardian. All of them had been part of the mass crossing from Morocco in late July that made headlines around the world.

stories.title: Deportees Sent to Liberia Recount Harrowing Details of U.S. Expulsion and Treatment by ICE
stories.summary: Ten deportees said they experienced or witnessed what they called abusive or violent treatment by ICE. They spent months in detention, they said, before being sent to nations where they had no ties.

stories.title: Au Niger, la tentative de coup d’Etat met en lumière les faiblesses de la junte du général Tiani
stories.summary: Après avoir été menacé durant une journée, le régime de Niamey est parvenu à mettre fin à une tentative de putsch, grâce à ses alliés russes de l’Africa Corps. Mais cette mutinerie révèle sa fragilité, alors que le pays est en proie aux attaques de plusieurs groupes djihadistes.

stories.title: Nurture not nature? How young women can learn to better wield economic power | Heather Stewart
stories.summary: Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given just 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks. Photograph: MBI/Alamy View image in fullscreen Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given just 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks. Photograph: MBI/Alamy How young women can learn to better wield economic power Heather Stewart Project in Zambia shows how teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects W omen making their way in patriarchal societies down the ages have always had to wield their meagre economic power deftly. New evidence from a fascinating research project in Zambia suggests that’s a skill that can be learned. A team of female US academics have been gathering data for more than a decade, which shows that teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects.

stories.title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
stories.summary: Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside. The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children. “The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety. The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.” The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

stories.title: Algérie : le président Tebboune veut appliquer la peine de mort contre les pyromanes
stories.summary: Publicité Algérie : le président Tebboune veut appliquer la peine de mort contre les pyromanes Afrique Le président algérien Abdelmadjid Tebboune a annoncé dimanche vouloir rétablir l'application de la peine de mort contre les pyromanes, après les incendies meurtriers qui ont ravagé l'est et le nord du pays. L'Algérie observe un moratoire sur la peine de mort depuis 1993. Publié le : 31/08/2026 - 09:00 2 min Temps de lecture Partager Par : FRANCE 24 Le président algérien Abdelmadjid Tebboune lors d'une conférence de presse à Berlin en Allemagne, le 16 juillet 2026. © John Macdougall, AFP Le président algérien Abdelmadjid Tebboune – dont le pays observe un moratoire sur la peine de mort depuis 1993 – a annoncé dimanche 30 août vouloir rétablir son application contre les pyromanes, après les incendies meurtriers qui ont ravagé l'est et le nord de l' Algérie cet été. S'adressant au ministre de la Justice lors d'une réunion consacrée aux feux en présence de hauts responsables civils et militaires, le chef de l'État algérien a ordonné "une modification du Code pénal" avant le 15 septembre. Abdelmadjid Tebboune a demandé à ce que le projet passe par le gouvernement, puis que le Parlement l'étudie "rapidement". "On réinstaure la condamnation à mort pour les pyromanes", a-t-il déclaré. "Il y aura exécution" une fois les voies de recours épuisées pour les condamnés, a-t-il insisté dans des images retransmises à la télévision.

stories.title: En Guinée-Bissau, un référendum constitutionnel et l’ombre du président déchu
stories.summary: A trois mois de l’élection présidentielle, le général Horta N’Tam, arrivé à la tête du pays par un putsch, en novembre 2025, entend instaurer un régime présidentiel à la place du régime parlementaire en vigueur. L’opposition a appelé au boycott du scrutin.

stories.title: La Somalie et la Turquie libèrent un cargo détourné au terme d’une opération meurtrière ; le Puntland dénonce le paiement d’une rançon
stories.summary: Cette opération a été menée dans un contexte de recrudescence des actes de piraterie au large de la Somalie, où au moins 15 attaques ont été recensées depuis le début de l’année, d’après une analyse de données de l’Organisation maritime internationale.

stories.title: Soldiers in Niger Attack Presidential Palace and Airport, Shaking Junta
stories.summary: Renegade Nigerien soldiers attacked sites around the capital, the defense ministry said, including a key air base that hosts Russian mercenaries.

stories.title: Le FMI et le Sénégal reprennent leur coopération, un prêt de 2,2 milliards de dollars en vue pour Dakar
stories.summary: Le FMI et le Sénégal reprennent leur coopération, un prêt de 2,2 milliards de dollars en vue pour Dakar Le Fonds monétaire international (FMI) et le Sénégal ont annoncé mardi 1er septembre un accord sur le principe d'un prêt de 2,2 milliards de dollars afin d'appuyer Dakar et de participer au rétablissement de la santé financière du pays aux prises d'une dette vertigineuse de 132 % du PIB. Publié le : 01/09/2026 - 17:30 Modifié le : 02/09/2026 - 06:38 3 min Temps de lecture Conférence de presse du ministre de l’Économie et des Finances, Cheikh Diba (au centre), sur la signature d’un accord avec le FMI. © Léa-Lisa Westerhoff / RFI Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Le FMI s'est réengagé, mardi 1er septembre 2026, à venir en aide au Sénégal et à lui prêter de l'argent, rapporte notre correspondante dans la capitale sénégalaise, Léa-Lisa Westerhoff . La décision a été prise près de deux ans après la suspension par l'instance financière de son dernier prêt – 1,8 milliard de dollars – en raison de la révélation par Dakar d'une dette cachée de plus de 9 milliards de dollars contractée par l'administration précédente. Cet accord « de 36 mois au titre de la Facilité élargie de crédit (FEC) d'un montant d'environ 2,2 milliards de dollars » doit être soumis à l'approbation du Conseil d'administration du FMI, précise l'institution dans un communiqué. Il est corrélé aussi à l'application de « mesures correctives résolues » pour éviter que des dettes publiques ne puissent de nouveau être dissimulées.

stories.title: Turkey and Israel Vie for Middle East Influence as Tensions Spike
stories.summary: Israel’s strike on a Syrian base to pre-empt the feared deployment of Turkish forces was part of a growing competition in the Middle East and beyond.

stories.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
stories.summary: The 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace. Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/Getty View image in fullscreen The 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace. Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/Getty Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty. Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions. The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

stories.title: Africa's aging autocrats fight to stay in power
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JK6k Backed by a loyal inner circle, Paul Biya (center) was sworn in for an eighth term as president of Cameroon in November 2025 Image: Angel Ngwe/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Power can be seductive, and many who possess it want to hold on for as long as possible. The leaders of China and Russia , for example, cleared the way for additional terms years ago, and in the United States, the president occasionally speaks of another run for office, even though the US Constitution does not allow it. From the perspective of Paul Biya, however, Chinese President Xi Jinping , Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump are still relatively new to office. Cameroon's president has been head of state since 1982. In 2025, Biya began his eighth term — which is officially due to end on November 6, 2032, just a few months before his 100th birthday.

stories.title: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, King Oyo ascended to the throne at the age of three but was crowned on reaching adulthood at 18 in 2010 By Swaibu Ibrahim BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kampala Published 28 August 2026 A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minister has announced. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father. The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US. Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power. Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch , external , ruled over more than two million people.

stories.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
stories.summary: Mark Zuckerberg was not forced to testify in the US lawsuit, which Meta settled on Wednesday. Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Mark Zuckerberg was not forced to testify in the US lawsuit, which Meta settled on Wednesday. Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty Images What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm? Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands I n October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

stories.title: ‘Behind every case, a person’: the man leading DRC’s Ebola fight on the human cost hidden behind the numbers
stories.summary: Congolese medical workers in PPE carry children tested and cleared of Ebola in Bunia town, Ituri province, DRC. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters View image in fullscreen Congolese medical workers in PPE carry children tested and cleared of Ebola in Bunia town, Ituri province, DRC. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Interview ‘Behind every case, a person’: the man leading DRC’s Ebola fight on the human cost hidden behind the numbers Tracy McVeigh Prof Pierre Akilimali, who heads DR Congo’s response to an outbreak that has so far killed more than 2,700 people, says tackling the disease requires trust and respect T he statistics, says the man responsible for overseeing the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), are meaningless. stories.title: 'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
stories.summary: Image caption, Fatima says her husband and six of his siblings were killed when bandits attacked By Yemisi Adegoke BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Zamfara and Oyo states Published 27 August 2026 "If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you." The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back. "They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service. It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom. Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people." About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima. She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
